# IFC5-Architecture-White-Paper.md comments

Hi Dennis. I don't agree with everything but I think this is a wonderful document in terms of uncovering the uncertainty and doubts in the group wrt to ifcx and these are exactly the points we need to advance on. Some notes:

1

> This creates a closed-world assumption: an entity has exactly one canonical position

I disagree, but agree it needs more elaboration because it is a nuanced subject. There is in fact nothing that prevents multiple side by side hierarchies. Hierarchies are assembled by means of referring to children by means of their paths. Typically these targets are just root-level definitions. By means of the incoming edge the child is no-longer rendered as an independent element, but by means of its child role. However, another hierarchy can exist that inserts the child in a different place. The path is not its identity, but an address. 

In case of hello wall you can refer to the Window as:
- 2c2d549f-f9fe-4e22-8590-562fda81a690
- /ab143723-f7b1-5368-b106-55896e88d768/My_Project/My_Site/My_Building/My_Storey/Wall/Window

And you could see the first one as the stable UUID irrespective of its location in the tree.

2

> The inherited USD composition model (LIVRPS precedence) resolves disagreements by having one opinion win

I agree we did badly initially in communicating about this. I think everyone agrees now that 'one opinion winning by means of order or strength' agrees never will become the modus operandi of ifcx. The superimposed trees is more about uncovering conflicts than resolving them.

3

> Incomplete relation coverage

The domain specific schema is not complete and also this should have been expressed more clearly.

However, there are no technical limitations in terms expressing relationships. See for example the systems example https://github.com/buildingSMART/IFC5-development/blob/main/examples/Domestic%20Hot%20Water/domestic-hot-water.ifcx#L1041

However, objectified relationships are deliberately no longer present. In the world of Express objectified relationships are a nice way to build in modularity, because by means of inverses and abstract supertypes you can create some sort of modularity within one global schema. In IFCX/ECS we already have components (with identity, provenance) as an additional mechanism, composition over inheritance *plus* objectified relationships is unnecessary.

4

> Any tool — including AI reasoning systems — must implement the USD composition engine before it can answer "what is this object?"

IFCX just makes this existing behaviour explicit. IFC4 has similar inheritance logic between TypeObject PropertySets and Occurences - just much more idiosyncratic and implicit in walls of text within the domain schemas. IFCX introduces this as a formalized first-principled solution. IFC4 beyond-taxonomy-compatibility therefore has the risk of inheriting this poorly formalized logic.

---
**louistrue** (2026-08-03):

Thanks Dennis. I read the paper, the schema, the IFCY Hello Wall and the RFC set, and parsed the two Hello Wall files against each other. Most of this comes from the artifacts rather than the prose.

First: anyone reading only the white paper will miss how much the RFC set is doing. RFC-041's capability-by-capability table is the clearest statement I have seen of what OWA actually demands of IFCX and ECS, and it is honest that neither has provenance, neither distinguishes unknown from absent, and neither has a delta format. That framing is worth more than the specific remedies.

Three things in the artifacts that look like open design questions.

**1. The component `id` currently has nothing to do.** §3.2 says it "enables components to be referenced, versioned, or superseded independently" and R5 puts it in the normative five-tuple, but the schema has it optional (`id?`) and in `hello-wall-ifcy.json` nothing references a component id — even the snapshots' `derivedFrom` arrays point at entity UUIDs. 64 component UUIDs, zero uses. The reason is that the schema has no `supersedes`, no `status`, no `validUntil`, no version and no content hash. You already have the questions that would fix it: RFC-033 Q3 (how are deleted objects represented) and RFC-041 Q6 (is a normative delta format needed now). Until those are answered the five-tuple is really a four-tuple.

**2. The schema and the paper give different answers to RFC-041 Q3.** Q3 asks whether resolution is "consumer defines a policy" or whether IFC5 defines precedence rules. §3.4.4 and R17 answer the first way: "No system-imposed resolution destroys information." But the schema documents `ProvenanceAuthority` as controlling "which assertions override others when packages are federated", ordered `survey > as-built > design-intent > inferred`. That is the second answer, and I do not think it got there by accident — as soon as you specify what a consumer does, a precedence order appears.

The ISO track constrains this. A conformance suite has to ask "what is the height of wall W?" and check the answer; if two conformant consumers may legitimately answer differently, that is an interoperability regression relative to IFC4. And `ProvenanceAuthority` being an open string union (`| string`) means even policy-by-authority cannot be pinned down normatively. What seems to survive both constraints: all opinions retained and attributed, plus a normative default resolution, plus an explicitly declarable policy. Nothing is destroyed and a conformance test still has a defined expected answer. That also gives Thomas's "surfacing conflicts rather than resolving them" a mechanism, which neither architecture has today.

**3. §3.4.3 and RFC-006 Q1.** §3.4.3 names the risk of carrying a `MaterialisedSnapshot` — "a second source of truth that can drift" — then answers it with discipline rather than mechanism. The snapshot carries `derivedFrom` and `resolvedAt`, so it records what it came from and when, but not whether the source has changed since. In the example both snapshots have already lost the instances' own `name` values, so the resolved view is incomplete relative to the composition it caches.

RFC-006 Q1 already asks whether canonical serialization is required, and already cites RFC 8785. That is the missing mechanism: a canonical content hash of the source, JCS plus SHA-256, written `sha256-<hex>`. In our prototype a derived representation carries the hash of what it came from and a consumer resolves it to `fresh`, `stale` or `unknown` — changing a profile dimension or moving a vertex flips it to stale, permuting key order does not, no hash reports unknown rather than fresh. The cached copy still displays, and reports stale. The consumer decides what to do about drift; the format has to make drift detectable, and `resolvedAt` alone does not. It would also give the `id` in point 1 a job: supersession becomes "this component supersedes id X, whose content hashed to H". Offered as a separable addition, not a criticism.

Two smaller notes: the §3.1.3 "normative typed-value form" `{"type": "IfcLabel", "value": …}` appears nowhere in either artifact, and R4's mandatory `fetchedAt` is absent from all nineteen URI references in the file, with the schema adding a separate `TaxonomyRef` without that field to accommodate it.

One correction that affects how R12 is weighed. §4.3 and the §4.8 table say IFCX's class attribute is a "flat string attribute; no supertype encoding". In the actual file `bsi::ifc::class` is `{code: "IfcWall", uri: "https://identifier.buildingsmart.org/uri/.../class/IfcWall"}` — the same bSDD URI your `taxonomy` ref carries, and §3.2 quotes that form correctly. R12's real delta is the offline cache, which I would make mandatory rather than optional; otherwise subtype-query correctness depends on network availability and on bSDD's own versioning, and a conformance suite can test neither.

Geometry I took to the RFC-014 discussion, since it already frames the question and asks for a prototype: https://github.com/Drshelden/IFCV5Work/discussions/3. Sub-element identity likewise, in the RFC-003 discussion: https://github.com/Drshelden/IFCV5Work/discussions/4.

One geometry point belongs here though, because it is specific to Layer 3. Once hierarchy is navigational only, it is not defined what `usd:XformComponent` composes against. `hello-wall-ifcy.json` moves the windows out from under the wall, where IFCX nests them, to directly under the storey, while keeping the same transform matrices. That works only because the wall's transform is identity. If the spatial view is non-authoritative, the spec has to say which graph is the transform-inheritance graph.

For scope on my side: everything I cite runs on our own post-alpha variant with external attribute tables, not on upstream IFCX, so it shows satisfiability rather than conformance. Several of your criticisms apply to us too — no per-assertion provenance, only a coarse section-level author and timestamp; no relation coverage at all, the work is geometry-only; and our table indirection means a node's geometry is not readable without our loader, a real trade against the schema-free parseability you value. No element-level GlobalId-stability story across restructuring and merge, and no delta or merge algorithm, only the change-detection primitive one needs.
